claim: Nodal signaling activity spans a normal range in the absence of signaling feedback and relay.
source: We find that Nodal signaling activity spans a normal range in the absence of signaling feedback and relay, suggesting that diffusion is sufficient for Nodal gradient formation.
evidence: Demonstrated through sensor cell assays in MZsmad2 mutants showing gradient formation without feedback (Figure 1C)

claim: Diffusion is sufficient for Nodal gradient formation.
source: We find that Nodal signaling activity spans a normal range in the absence of signaling feedback and relay, suggesting that diffusion is sufficient for Nodal gradient formation.
evidence: Inferred from sensor cell assays showing normal gradient range in MZsmad2 mutants lacking feedback

claim: The range of endogenous Nodal ligands is set by the EGF-CFC co-receptor Oep.
source: We further show that the range of endogenous Nodal ligands is set by the EGF-CFC co-receptor Oep: in the absence of Oep, Nodal activity spreads to form a nearly uniform distribution throughout the embryo.
evidence: Demonstrated by sensor cell assays in MZoep mutants showing expanded Nodal signaling range (Figure 2B)

claim: In the absence of Oep, Nodal activity spreads to form a nearly uniform distribution throughout the embryo.
source: We further show that the range of endogenous Nodal ligands is set by the EGF-CFC co-receptor Oep: in the absence of Oep, Nodal activity spreads to form a nearly uniform distribution throughout the embryo.
evidence: Shown by sensor cell detection of Nodal at the animal pole in MZoep embryos (Figure 2D,E)

claim: Increasing Oep levels sensitizes cells to Nodal ligands.
source: In turn, increasing Oep levels sensitizes cells to Nodal ligands.
evidence: Demonstrated by oep-overexpressing sensor cells showing enhanced pSmad2 staining compared to neighbors (Figure 3B)

claim: Oep regulates the diffusive spread of Nodal ligands by setting the rate of capture by target cells.
source: This model predicts, and we confirm in vivo, the surprising observation that a failure to replenish Oep transforms the Nodal signaling gradient into a travelling wave.
evidence: Supported by computational model that reproduces experimental observations (Figure 4) and confirmed by traveling wave in Zoep mutants (Figure 5E)

claim: A failure to replenish Oep transforms the Nodal signaling gradient into a travelling wave.
source: This model predicts, and we confirm in vivo, the surprising observation that a failure to replenish Oep transforms the Nodal signaling gradient into a travelling wave.
evidence: Observed in zygotic oep mutants showing propagating wave of signaling from dome to shield stage (Figure 5E)

claim: Patterns of Nodal morphogen signaling are shaped by co-receptor-mediated restriction of ligand spread and sensitization of responding cells.
source: These results reveal that patterns of Nodal morphogen signaling are shaped by co-receptor-mediated restriction of ligand spread and sensitization of responding cells.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple experimental observations showing Oep's role in regulating range and sensitivity

claim: Mvg1 sensor cells accurately report on their local signaling environment.
source: The Mvg1 sensors exhibited α-pSmad2 staining intensity similar to their wild-type neighbors, and quantification of staining across replicate embryos revealed similar signaling gradients for host and sensor cells (Figure 1B, lower panel; blue and red points, respectively). This result demonstrates that transplanted sensor cells accurately report on their local signaling environment.
evidence: Demonstrated by comparing sensor and host cell pSmad2 staining in wild-type hosts (Figure 1B)

claim: Sensor cell migration after transplant does not compromise the assay.
source: We further note that sensor cell migration after transplant does not appear to compromise the assay, as sensor cells exhibit signaling intensities appropriate for their position at the time of embryo fixation.
evidence: Inferred from sensor cells showing position-appropriate signaling intensities

claim: Cell rearrangement at the margin is minimal prior to gastrulation.
source: This outcome is consistent with previous observations that cell rearrangement at the margin is minimal prior to gastrulation (Dubrulle et al., 2015; Helde et al., 1994; Wilson et al., 1993).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: YSL-derived Nodal ligands can form a gradient of normal range without help from signaling feedback and relay.
source: Together, these experiments suggest that YSL-derived Nodal ligands can form a gradient of normal range without help from signaling feedback and relay.
evidence: Concluded from sensor cell assays in MZsmad2 mutants showing normal gradient range (Figure 1C)

claim: MZsmad2 embryos lack pSmad2.
source: We verified that MZsmad2 embryos lack pSmad2 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) but continue to express cyclops and squint in the YSL (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Verified by immunostaining shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: MZsmad2 embryos continue to express cyclops and squint in the YSL.
source: We verified that MZsmad2 embryos lack pSmad2 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) but continue to express cyclops and squint in the YSL (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Verified by smFISH shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2

claim: Expression of both Nodals was excluded from the blastoderm in MZsmad2 mutants.
source: Expression of both Nodals was excluded from the blastoderm, confirming that these mutants are incapable of Nodal autoregulation (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Shown by smFISH in Figure 1—figure supplement 2

claim: MZsmad2 mutants are incapable of Nodal autoregulation.
source: Expression of both Nodals was excluded from the blastoderm, confirming that these mutants are incapable of Nodal autoregulation (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Inferred from absence of nodal expression in blastoderm shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2

claim: The half-distance of the Nodal signaling gradient in MZsmad2 hosts is 45 μm.
source: Quantification of staining in MZsmad2 hosts (Figure 1C, lower panel) revealed a Nodal signaling gradient similar in range to that of wild-type controls (Figure 1B., lower panel; half-distances of 45 and 37 μm for MZsmad2 and wild type, respectively).
evidence: Measured from quantification of sensor cell assays (Figure 1C)

claim: The half-distance of the Nodal signaling gradient in wild-type hosts is 37 μm.
source: Quantification of staining in MZsmad2 hosts (Figure 1C, lower panel) revealed a Nodal signaling gradient similar in range to that of wild-type controls (Figure 1B., lower panel; half-distances of 45 and 37 μm for MZsmad2 and wild type, respectively).
evidence: Measured from quantification of sensor cell assays (Figure 1B)

claim: Ligand mobility may be hindered by interaction with extracellular factors.
source: Biophysical studies with GFP-tagged Nodals suggest that ligand mobility may be hindered by interaction with extracellular factors, as measured diffusion rates for both Cyclops and Squint are >10 fold lower than for free GFP (Müller et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to biophysical studies

claim: Measured diffusion rates for both Cyclops and Squint are >10 fold lower than for free GFP.
source: Biophysical studies with GFP-tagged Nodals suggest that ligand mobility may be hindered by interaction with extracellular factors, as measured diffusion rates for both Cyclops and Squint are >10 fold lower than for free GFP (Müller et al., 2012).
evidence: Cited from previous biophysical studies

claim: Cell surface receptor complexes are candidates for hindering Nodal mobility.
source: Cell surface receptor complexes are clear candidates for this role (Wang et al., 2016), because transient ligand capture or receptor-mediated endocytosis could constrain the gradient (Wartlick et al., 2009), and receptors have been shown to regulate gradient range for other signals (Baeg et al., 2004; Chen and Struhl, 1996; Lecuit and Cohen, 1998; Okabe et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on receptor-mediated gradient regulation

claim: Transient ligand capture or receptor-mediated endocytosis could constrain the gradient.
source: Cell surface receptor complexes are clear candidates for this role (Wang et al., 2016), because transient ligand capture or receptor-mediated endocytosis could constrain the gradient (Wartlick et al., 2009), and receptors have been shown to regulate gradient range for other signals (Baeg et al., 2004; Chen and Struhl, 1996; Lecuit and Cohen, 1998; Okabe et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to theoretical and experimental studies

claim: Receptors have been shown to regulate gradient range for other signals.
source: Cell surface receptor complexes are clear candidates for this role (Wang et al., 2016), because transient ligand capture or receptor-mediated endocytosis could constrain the gradient (Wartlick et al., 2009), and receptors have been shown to regulate gradient range for other signals (Baeg et al., 2004; Chen and Struhl, 1996; Lecuit and Cohen, 1998; Okabe et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on Dpp, Hh, Wg, and other morphogens

claim: Loss of Oep leads to an expanded range of action for both Cyclops and Squint.
source: To test whether loss of Oep affects both Nodal ligands similarly, we performed sensor cell assays in MZoep;sqt and MZoep;cyc double mutants. Loss of Oep led to an expanded range of action for both Cyclops (i.e. in MZoep;sqt mutants) and Squint (i.e. in MZoep;cyc mutants), and the signaling ranges in both double mutants were comparable to that observed in the MZoep single mutant (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by sensor cell assays in double mutants shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: The signaling ranges in MZoep;sqt and MZoep;cyc double mutants are comparable to that observed in the MZoep single mutant.
source: Loss of Oep led to an expanded range of action for both Cyclops (i.e. in MZoep;sqt mutants) and Squint (i.e. in MZoep;cyc mutants), and the signaling ranges in both double mutants were comparable to that observed in the MZoep single mutant (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Shown by comparison of sensor cell assays in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: Long-range Nodal signaling in oep mutants does not reflect residual Nodal signaling between Mvg1 sensor cells.
source: We note that long-range Nodal signaling in oep mutants does not reflect residual Nodal signaling between Mvg1 sensor cells, as signaling intensity was independent of sensor cell density (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Demonstrated by analysis showing no correlation between neighbor number and signaling intensity in Figure 2—figure supplement 2

claim: Direct ligand visualization revealed an expanded range of secreted Nodal in MZoep mutants compared to wild type.
source: Although endogenous Nodal ligands have not been detectable to date and the sensor assay is the most sensitive reporter for signaling by Nodal ligands, we ectopically expressed GFP-tagged Squint in a transplanted clone of source cells. Direct ligand visualization also revealed an expanded range of secreted Nodal in MZoep mutants compared to wild type (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Shown by Squint-sfGFP gradient measurements in Figure 2—figure supplement 3

claim: The expansion of the signaling gradient in lefty1;lefty2 mutant embryos is mild compared to observations in MZoep embryos.
source: For example, the expansion of the signaling gradient in lefty1;lefty2 mutant embryos, which lack negative feedback on Nodal signaling (Rogers et al., 2017; Figure 2C), is mild compared to our observations in MZoep embryos (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: Shown by comparison of sensor cell assays in Figure 2B and 2C

claim: Receptor complexes play key roles in constraining the spread of Nodal signals from the YSL.
source: These results demonstrate that receptor complexes play key roles in constraining the spread of Nodal signals from the YSL.
evidence: Concluded from sensor cell assays showing dramatic gradient expansion in MZoep mutants

claim: EGF-CFC proteins such as Oep are typically regarded as permissive factors for Nodal signaling.
source: EGF-CFC proteins such as Oep are typically regarded as permissive factors for Nodal signaling. Oep facilitates the assembly of receptor-ligand complexes but is not thought to regulate signaling beyond conferring competence (Zhang et al., 1998).
evidence: Represents established scientific consensus cited from literature

claim: Oep facilitates the assembly of receptor-ligand complexes but is not thought to regulate signaling beyond conferring competence.
source: Oep facilitates the assembly of receptor-ligand complexes but is not thought to regulate signaling beyond conferring competence (Zhang et al., 1998).
evidence: Represents established view from literature

claim: Oep levels set the rate of capture of diffusing Nodal ligands.
source: The simplest way to accommodate this result is to stipulate that Oep levels set the rate of capture of diffusing Nodal ligands.
evidence: Proposed mechanism to explain experimental observations

claim: Oep could control the range of Nodal activity by regulating the rate of receptor-mediated ligand internalization.
source: Through this mechanism, Oep could control the range of Nodal activity by regulating the rate of receptor-mediated ligand internalization (i.e. the effective ligand degradation rate).
evidence: Proposed mechanism based on theoretical considerations

claim: Increasing Oep levels should enhance cell sensitivity to Nodal ligands by facilitating capture by receptor complexes.
source: This model makes two testable predictions. First, increasing Oep levels should enhance cell sensitivity to Nodal ligands by facilitating capture by receptor complexes.
evidence: Prediction from theoretical model

claim: Increasing Oep levels should reduce the range of Nodal signaling by increasing the effective degradation rate.
source: Second, increasing Oep levels should reduce the range of Nodal signaling by increasing the effective degradation rate.
evidence: Prediction from theoretical model

claim: Sensors with increased Oep levels stain more brightly for pSmad2 than neighboring host cells.
source: Sensors with increased Oep levels stained more brightly for pSmad2 than neighboring host cells (Figure 3B), while sensors injected with gfp alone matched the behavior of their neighbors (Figure 3A).
evidence: Shown by sensor cell assays in Figure 3B

claim: The oep-overexpressing sensors detected Nodal further from the margin than the host cells.
source: Interestingly, we found that the oep-overexpressing sensors detected Nodal further from the margin than the host cells, suggesting that the Nodal ligand gradient extends beyond the domain of detectable signaling in normal embryos (Figure 3B).
evidence: Observed in sensor cell assays shown in Figure 3B

claim: The Nodal ligand gradient extends beyond the domain of detectable signaling in normal embryos.
source: Interestingly, we found that the oep-overexpressing sensors detected Nodal further from the margin than the host cells, suggesting that the Nodal ligand gradient extends beyond the domain of detectable signaling in normal embryos (Figure 3B).
evidence: Inferred from oep-overexpressing sensors detecting Nodal beyond normal range

claim: The increased sensitivity of the oep-overexpressing sensors does not reflect the action of hyperactive-positive feedback on Nodal production.
source: We note that the increased sensitivity of the oep-overexpressing sensors does not reflect the action of hyperactive-positive feedback on Nodal production, as Mvg1 cells are incapable of producing functional Nodal-Vg1 heterodimers.
evidence: Inferred from known properties of Mvg1 cells

claim: Mvg1 cells are incapable of producing functional Nodal-Vg1 heterodimers.
source: We note that the increased sensitivity of the oep-overexpressing sensors does not reflect the action of hyperactive-positive feedback on Nodal production, as Mvg1 cells are incapable of producing functional Nodal-Vg1 heterodimers.
evidence: Established property of Mvg1 mutant cells

claim: In addition to being required for signaling competence, Oep regulates sensitivity to Nodal ligands.
source: These results suggest that, in addition to being required for signaling competence, Oep regulates sensitivity to Nodal ligands.
evidence: Concluded from oep overexpression experiments showing enhanced sensitivity

claim: Overexpression of Oep reduced the range and intensity of Nodal signaling in MZsmad2 hosts.
source: We performed sensor cell assays in MZsmad2 hosts injected with oep mRNA at the one-cell stage. Overexpression of Oep indeed reduced the range and intensity of Nodal signaling (Figure 3D) when compared with uninjected hosts (Figure 3C).
evidence: Shown by sensor cell assays in Figure 3C and 3D

claim: Overexpression of oep resulted in marked shortening of the Squint-sfGFP gradient relative to MZoep.
source: In the first experiment, we visualized the range of Squint-sfGFP gradients generated by transplanted source cells in hosts lacking oep (MZoep) and hosts overexpressing oep (MZoep injected with oep mRNA). Consistent with our sensor cell results, overexpression of oep resulted in marked shortening of the Squint-sfGFP gradient relative to MZoep (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Shown by direct visualization of Squint-sfGFP in Figure 2—figure supplement 3

claim: Halo-tagged ligand accumulated in the animal pole sensors in MZoep hosts but not in wild-type hosts.
source: Halo-tagged ligand accumulated in the animal pole sensors in MZoep hosts but not in wild-type hosts. This accumulation was prevented by overexpressing oep in the MZoep hosts.
evidence: Shown by Halo-tagged ligand visualization in Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: Accumulation of Halo-tagged ligand in MZoep hosts was prevented by overexpressing oep.
source: This accumulation was prevented by overexpressing oep in the MZoep hosts.
evidence: Shown by Halo-tagged ligand visualization in Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: Oep regulates both the range and intensity of Nodal signaling.
source: Together, these results indicate that Oep regulates both the range and intensity of Nodal signaling.
evidence: Concluded from multiple experiments showing Oep's effects on gradient range and cell sensitivity

claim: A simple mathematical model of Nodal gradient formation incorporating Oep-mediated capture reproduces experimental observations.
source: We formulated a simple mathematical model of Nodal gradient formation to explore whether Oep-mediated capture of diffusing Nodal ligands is sufficient to explain our experimental data (Figure 4A).
evidence: Demonstrated by computational simulations shown in Figure 4

claim: The simple model reproduces a signaling gradient with a scale and shape consistent with observations in wild-type embryos.
source: This simple model reproduces a signaling gradient with a scale and shape consistent with our observations in wild-type embryos (Figure 4B).
evidence: Shown by simulation results in Figure 4B

claim: A model in which Nodal capture rate is set by Oep concentration can reproduce the major experimental findings.
source: A model in which Nodal capture rate is set by Oep concentration can therefore reproduce our major experimental findings.
evidence: Concluded from simulations reproducing wild-type, MZoep, and oep overexpression conditions

claim: Maintaining receptors at high concentration could prevent ligand from traveling long distances before capture.
source: For example, maintaining receptors at high concentration would preclude depletion but could also prevent ligand from traveling long distances before capture.
evidence: Theoretical consideration about receptor dynamics

claim: Continually replacing receptor components as they are consumed by ligand binding could avoid receptor depletion.
source: Another way for the embryo to avoid depletion would be to continually replace receptor components as they are consumed by ligand binding.
evidence: Theoretical consideration about receptor dynamics

claim: Simulations incorporating receptor production and consumption generate stable exponential gradients.
source: Simulations incorporating receptor production and consumption generate stable exponential gradients (Figure 5B) with length scales comparable to our measurements in zebrafish embryos.
evidence: Shown by simulation results in Figure 5B

claim: Simulations with finite co-receptor supply generate a traveling wave of Nodal signaling that propagates outward from the ligand source.
source: To test the consequences of losing co-receptor replacement, we simulated gradient formation in a system that begins with a finite supply of free receptors that are not replaced. This change results in a surprising transformation of Nodal signaling dynamics; simulations with finite co-receptor supply generate a traveling wave of Nodal signaling that propagates outward from the ligand source (Figure 5C, magenta).
evidence: Shown by simulation results in Figure 5C

claim: The traveling wave dynamics reflect the gradual consumption of co-receptors due to ligand binding and subsequent endocytosis.
source: These dynamics reflect the gradual consumption of co-receptors due to ligand binding and subsequent endocytosis (Figure 5C, cyan).
evidence: Explained by simulation results showing receptor depletion in Figure 5C

claim: Wave formation does not critically depend on assumptions regarding the mechanism of co-receptor downregulation.
source: We note that wave formation does not critically depend on our assumptions regarding the mechanism of co-receptor downregulation; a model that incorporates Oep trafficking and recycling also supports our key conclusions (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Shown by alternative model simulations in Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: Co-receptor replenishment is a key determinant of the Nodal gradient shape.
source: In sum, these simulations raise the possibility that co-receptor replenishment is a key determinant of the Nodal gradient shape.
evidence: Concluded from simulations showing different dynamics with and without receptor replacement

claim: Zoep mutants begin with a finite supply of maternally provided oep mRNA but cannot express additional oep from the zygotic genome.
source: This background reproduces the key assumptions of the model above: Zoep mutants begin with a finite supply of maternally provided oep mRNA but cannot express additional oep from the zygotic genome (Zhang et al., 1998).
evidence: Established property of Zoep mutants cited from literature

claim: Maternally deposited oep mRNA is undetectable in Zoep mutants by germ ring stage.
source: Indeed, previous studies have shown that maternally deposited oep mRNA is undetectable in Zoep mutants by germ ring stage (Zhang et al., 1998) and that oep mRNA is depleted from wild-type embryos by 60% epiboly in the absence of zygotic transcription (Vopalensky et al., 2018).
evidence: Cited from previous studies

claim: oep mRNA is depleted from wild-type embryos by 60% epiboly in the absence of zygotic transcription.
source: Indeed, previous studies have shown that maternally deposited oep mRNA is undetectable in Zoep mutants by germ ring stage (Zhang et al., 1998) and that oep mRNA is depleted from wild-type embryos by 60% epiboly in the absence of zygotic transcription (Vopalensky et al., 2018).
evidence: Cited from previous studies

claim: The wild-type Nodal signaling profile monotonically decreases from the margin, decaying to background over ~8 cell tiers.
source: Consistent with previous observations, the wild-type Nodal signaling profile monotonically decreases from the margin, decaying to background over ~8 cell tiers (Figure 5D).
evidence: Shown by immunostaining time course in Figure 5D

claim: In Zoep mutants, Nodal signaling is restricted to the margin at dome stage but propagates outward to form a broad band of signaling by shield stage.
source: Strikingly, in Zoep mutants, Nodal signaling is restricted to the margin at dome stage (Figure 5E, left), but propagates outward to form a broad band of signaling by shield stage (Figure 5E, right).
evidence: Shown by immunostaining time course in Figure 5E

claim: Loss of co-receptor replacement transforms a steady-state exponential gradient into a wave of Nodal signaling that propagates toward the animal pole.
source: As predicted by the model, loss of co-receptor replacement by zygotic expression thus transforms a steady-state exponential gradient into a wave of Nodal signaling that propagates toward the animal pole.
evidence: Concluded from comparison of model predictions and Zoep mutant observations

claim: Overall signaling intensity is lower in Zoep mutants due to lower overall co-receptor levels.
source: We note that, in accordance with model simulations, overall signaling intensity is lower in Zoep mutants due to lower overall co-receptor levels (Figure 5F).
evidence: Shown by comparison of staining intensities in Figure 5F

claim: Continued co-receptor replacement is important in shaping the pattern of Nodal signaling.
source: These results highlight the importance of continued co-receptor replacement in shaping the pattern of Nodal signaling.
evidence: Concluded from Zoep mutant experiments showing wave formation without receptor replacement

claim: Endogenous Nodals secreted from the YSL can drive signaling over a normal range in the absence of feedback and relay mechanisms.
source: We find that endogenous Nodals secreted from the YSL can drive signaling over a normal range in the absence of feedback and relay mechanisms (Figure 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by sensor cell assays in MZsmad2 mutants

claim: Expression of Oep regulates the spread, potency, and shape of Nodal activity.
source: We go on to demonstrate that expression of Oep, a Nodal co-receptor, regulates the spread (Figure 2), potency (Figure 3), and shape (Figure 5) of Nodal activity.
evidence: Demonstrated by multiple experiments shown in Figures 2, 3, and 5

claim: A simple computational model explains the Nodal signaling gradient in terms of free ligand diffusion and binding to cell surface receptor complexes.
source: We present a simple computational model that explains the Nodal signaling gradient in terms of free ligand diffusion and binding to cell surface receptor complexes (Figure 4).
evidence: Demonstrated by computational simulations in Figure 4

claim: In the computational model, Oep regulates the range of ligand spread and sensitivity of embryonic cells by setting the rate of ligand capture.
source: In this description, Oep regulates the range of ligand spread and sensitivity of embryonic cells by setting the rate of ligand capture.
evidence: Proposed mechanism based on computational model

claim: Diffusion has long been regarded as an attractive mechanism for signal dispersal in tissues.
source: Diffusion has long been regarded as an attractive mechanism for signal dispersal in tissues (Crick, 1970).
evidence: Represents established scientific consensus

claim: Signaling patterns consistent with simple diffusion-degradation mechanisms are common in developing tissues.
source: Indeed, signaling patterns consistent with simple diffusion-degradation mechanisms—for example single-exponential gradients with length scales of ~10–100 µm— are common in developing tissues (Kicheva et al., 2012).
evidence: Cited from literature review

claim: It has been argued that diffusible ligands would be impractical to contain without physical boundaries.
source: For example, it has been argued that diffusible ligands would be impractical to contain without physical boundaries (Kornberg and Guha, 2007), and that diffusion-driven gradients would not be a reliable source of positional information (Wolpert, 2016).
evidence: Cited from theoretical arguments in literature

claim: Diffusion-driven gradients would not be a reliable source of positional information.
source: For example, it has been argued that diffusible ligands would be impractical to contain without physical boundaries (Kornberg and Guha, 2007), and that diffusion-driven gradients would not be a reliable source of positional information (Wolpert, 2016).
evidence: Cited from theoretical arguments in literature

claim: This study is the first to examine the shape of the Nodal signaling gradient in the absence of feedback and relay.
source: However, it has not been possible to clearly test whether feedback is required for the dispersal of endogenous ligands. This study is the first to examine the shape of the Nodal signaling gradient in the absence of feedback and relay.
evidence: Authors' assessment of novelty of their work

claim: A gradient of approximately normal range and shape can form even when feedback is disabled.
source: We found that a gradient of approximately normal range and shape can form even when feedback is disabled.
evidence: Concluded from sensor cell assays in MZsmad2 mutants

claim: Recent studies in zebrafish embryos and human gastruloids have proposed that long-range Nodal signaling relies on a positive feedback-driven relay.
source: Recent studies in zebrafish embryos (van Boxtel et al., 2015) and human gastruloids (Liu, 2021) have proposed that long-range Nodal signaling relies on a positive feedback-driven relay.
evidence: Cited from recent literature

claim: Nodal signaling induces nodal gene expression.
source: In zebrafish, this conclusion was based on the observations that Nodal signaling induces nodal gene expression (Meno et al., 1999) and the expression domain of a synthetic Nodal reporter gene coincides with, but does not extend beyond, the nodal expression domain (van Boxtel et al., 2015).
evidence: Cited from previous studies

claim: Previous zebrafish studies did not test whether the range of Nodal signaling depends on nodal autoregulation.
source: While these findings are consistent with relay-driven transport, these previous zebrafish studies did not test whether the range of Nodal signaling indeed depends on nodal autoregulation and contracts when autoinduction is disrupted.
evidence: Authors' critique of previous studies

claim: Relay mechanisms are not necessary for the generation of a Nodal signaling gradient in zebrafish.
source: Our findings directly address this question and reveal that relay mechanisms are not necessary for the generation of a Nodal signaling gradient in zebrafish.
evidence: Concluded from sensor cell assays in MZsmad2 mutants

claim: Nodal gene expression in the YSL is sufficient to establish a Nodal signaling gradient.
source: Nodal gene expression in the YSL is sufficient to establish a Nodal signaling gradient.
evidence: Concluded from sensor cell assays showing gradient formation from YSL-derived Nodals

claim: In human gastruloids, Nodal signaling is attenuated when receiver cells are nodal mutants.
source: In human gastruloids, engineered gradients created with juxtaposed 'sender' and 'receiver' cells revealed that Nodal signaling is attenuated when receiver cells are nodal mutants (Liu, 2021).
evidence: Cited from study on human gastruloids

claim: It remains unclear if autoregulation is required for maintaining the initial nodal source or for generating a relay of nodal expression in human gastruloids.
source: This experiment demonstrates that nodal autoregulation supports the spread of Nodal signaling; however, since nodal expression in sender cells was also reduced in this context, it remains unclear if autoregulation is required for maintaining the initial nodal source or for generating a relay of nodal expression.
evidence: Authors' interpretation of limitations of cited study

claim: Different tissues may require distinct implementations of the Nodal-Lefty patterning system.
source: It is conceivable that different tissues require distinct implementations of the Nodal-Lefty patterning system.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of differences between systems

claim: The rapid pace of zebrafish mesendodermal patterning may make diffusion the only viable Nodal transport mechanism.
source: For example, the rapid pace of zebrafish mesendodermal patterning may make diffusion the only viable Nodal transport mechanism, while slower development in mammalian embryos may permit the use of multi-step, feedback-driven transport mechanisms.
evidence: Speculative explanation for differences between zebrafish and mammalian systems

claim: Slower development in mammalian embryos may permit the use of multi-step, feedback-driven transport mechanisms.
source: For example, the rapid pace of zebrafish mesendodermal patterning may make diffusion the only viable Nodal transport mechanism, while slower development in mammalian embryos may permit the use of multi-step, feedback-driven transport mechanisms.
evidence: Speculative explanation for differences between zebrafish and mammalian systems

claim: Oep has been traditionally regarded as a permissive factor for signaling.
source: Our study identifies new roles for EGF-CFC co-receptors in Nodal signaling. Oep has been traditionally regarded as a permissive factor for signaling Zhang et al., 1998; it facilitates Nodal association with Activin receptors (Cheng et al., 2003; Reissmann et al., 2001; Yeo and Whitman, 2001) but was not thought to regulate gradient shape or cell sensitivity (Gritsman et al., 1999; Zhang et al., 1998).
evidence: Represents established view from literature

claim: Oep facilitates Nodal association with Activin receptors.
source: Oep has been traditionally regarded as a permissive factor for signaling Zhang et al., 1998; it facilitates Nodal association with Activin receptors (Cheng et al., 2003; Reissmann et al., 2001; Yeo and Whitman, 2001) but was not thought to regulate gradient shape or cell sensitivity (Gritsman et al., 1999; Zhang et al., 1998).
evidence: Cited from previous studies

claim: Oep was not thought to regulate gradient shape or cell sensitivity.
source: Oep has been traditionally regarded as a permissive factor for signaling Zhang et al., 1998; it facilitates Nodal association with Activin receptors (Cheng et al., 2003; Reissmann et al., 2001; Yeo and Whitman, 2001) but was not thought to regulate gradient shape or cell sensitivity (Gritsman et al., 1999; Zhang et al., 1998).
evidence: Represents previous understanding from literature

claim: Similar to receptors for Dpp, Hh and Wg, Oep is a key determinant of the mobility and potency of its cognate ligand.
source: Our observations suggest that— similar to receptors for Dpp (Lecuit and Cohen, 1998), Hh (Chen and Struhl, 1996) and Wg (Baeg et al., 2004)—Oep is a key determinant of the mobility and potency of its cognate ligand.
evidence: Concluded from experimental observations and comparison to other morphogen systems

claim: Oep is one of the strongest regulators of Nodal range yet discovered.
source: Indeed, far from being a bystander in gradient formation, Oep is one of the strongest regulators of Nodal range yet discovered.
evidence: Concluded from dramatic gradient expansion in MZoep mutants

claim: GFP-tagged Cyclops and Squint diffuse substantially slower than free GFP.
source: GFP-tagged Cyclops and Squint diffuse substantially slower than free GFP, whereas tagged Lefty proteins diffuse rapidly (Müller et al., 2012).
evidence: Cited from previous biophysical studies

claim: Tagged Lefty proteins diffuse rapidly.
source: GFP-tagged Cyclops and Squint diffuse substantially slower than free GFP, whereas tagged Lefty proteins diffuse rapidly (Müller et al., 2012).
evidence: Cited from previous biophysical studies

claim: The differential diffusivity of Nodal and Lefty proteins may originate in rates of capture by available receptor complexes.
source: Our data raise the possibility that the differential diffusivity of Nodal and Lefty proteins originates in rates of capture by available receptor complexes.
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on experimental findings

claim: Close to the Nodal source, Oep binds Nodal and stimulates signaling.
source: Oep-mediated ligand capture and signaling sensitization results in short-range enhancement and long-range inhibition of Nodal signaling: close to the Nodal source, Oep binds Nodal and stimulates signaling, whereas far from the source, little Nodal is available due to Oep-mediated capture close to the source.
evidence: Inferred from experimental observations of Oep's dual effects

claim: Far from the Nodal source, little Nodal is available due to Oep-mediated capture close to the source.
source: Oep-mediated ligand capture and signaling sensitization results in short-range enhancement and long-range inhibition of Nodal signaling: close to the Nodal source, Oep binds Nodal and stimulates signaling, whereas far from the source, little Nodal is available due to Oep-mediated capture close to the source.
evidence: Inferred from experimental observations of Oep's dual effects

claim: Despite its distinct molecular roles, the Nodal signaling factor Oep has a function reminiscent of the Nodal inhibitor Lefty.
source: Despite its distinct molecular roles, the Nodal signaling factor Oep thus has a function reminiscent of the Nodal inhibitor Lefty.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of Oep and Lefty effects on signaling range

claim: Lefty is produced at the margin, but diffuses rapidly to inhibit Nodal signaling far from the source.
source: Lefty is produced at the margin, but diffuses rapidly to inhibit Nodal signaling far from the source.
evidence: Represents established knowledge about Lefty function

claim: A common theme for Nodal regulators is to counteract the inherent potential for long-range Nodal diffusion and signaling.
source: A common theme for Nodal regulators is therefore to counteract the inherent potential for long-range Nodal diffusion and signaling and to restrict Nodal signaling to a domain near the ligand source.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of Oep and Lefty functions

claim: Without receptor replacement, the Nodal signaling pattern is qualitatively transformed from a stable gradient into a propagating wave.
source: We found that, without this replacement, the Nodal signaling pattern is qualitatively transformed from a stable gradient into a propagating wave.
evidence: Demonstrated by observations in Zoep mutants

claim: A signaling wave of the type observed in Zoep mutants was predicted in a theoretical study by Kerszberg and Wolpert, 1998.
source: Interestingly, a signaling wave of this type was predicted in a theoretical study of morphogen gradient formation by Kerszberg and Wolpert, 1998.
evidence: Cited from theoretical study

claim: Kerszberg and Wolpert used the wave phenomenon to argue that receptor saturation would make stable gradients difficult to achieve by diffusive transport.
source: In fact, they used this phenomenon to argue that receptor saturation would make stable gradients difficult to achieve by diffusive transport.
evidence: Cited from theoretical study

claim: Consumption of receptors can create unstable wave behavior.
source: Our results suggest that consumption of receptors can create precisely this type of unstable behavior, but that the embryo achieves a stable gradient through continual turnover of the receptor pool.
evidence: Concluded from Zoep mutant observations and simulations

claim: The embryo achieves a stable gradient through continual turnover of the receptor pool.
source: Our results suggest that consumption of receptors can create precisely this type of unstable behavior, but that the embryo achieves a stable gradient through continual turnover of the receptor pool.
evidence: Concluded from comparison of wild-type and Zoep mutant observations

claim: Consumption of Oep by Nodal might support the anterior spread of the expression of the Nodal gene southpaw in left-right patterning.
source: Though not employed during mesendodermal patterning, this phenomenon could provide a simple means of repurposing the Nodal patterning circuit to create dynamic waves of signaling in other contexts. For example, in left-right patterning the consumption of Oep by Nodal might support the anterior spread of the expression of the Nodal gene southpaw (Long et al., 2003).
evidence: Speculative proposal based on findings

claim: Signaling waves have emerged as a mechanism to coordinate diverse processes such as cell migration, tissue regeneration, and apoptosis.
source: More generally, signaling waves have emerged as a mechanism to coordinate diverse processes such as cell migration (Aoki et al., 2017), tissue regeneration (De Simone et al., 2021), and apoptosis (Cheng and Ferrell, 2018).
evidence: Cited from studies on signaling waves in various contexts

claim: Signaling feedback is generally invoked to explain signaling wave phenomena.
source: Signaling feedback is generally invoked to explain these phenomena.
evidence: Represents common explanation in the field

claim: Receptor depletion is an alternative, feedback-free mechanism of signaling wave formation.
source: However, our results suggest receptor depletion as an alternative, feedback-free mechanism of signaling wave formation.
evidence: Proposed based on findings in Zoep mutants

claim: The precise dynamics of Oep replacement might contribute additional interesting functions to patterning systems.
source: Finally, we speculate that the precise dynamics of Oep replacement might contribute additional interesting functions to patterning systems.
evidence: Speculative proposal

claim: Signaling-dependent receptor expression could confer robustness to fluctuations in source-derived morphogen production.
source: For example, signaling-dependent receptor expression could confer robustness to fluctuations in source-derived morphogen production (Barkai and Shilo, 2009; Eldar et al., 2003).
evidence: Speculative proposal supported by citations to theoretical work

claim: Lefty-mediated feedback was dispensable for normal development in zebrafish.
source: The surprising dispensability of positive feedback for gradient formation parallels our findings on the role of negative feedback in Nodal patterning (Rogers et al., 2017). In that work, we showed that Lefty-mediated feedback—despite its extensive conservation across animals—was dispensable for normal development in zebrafish.
evidence: Cited from previous work by the authors

claim: Lefty was required for robustness in Nodal patterning.
source: Lefty was instead required for robustness; intact feedback loops enabled the embryo to correct exogenous perturbations to signaling.
evidence: Cited from previous work by the authors

claim: Nodal positive feedback may serve a similar purpose to Lefty-mediated negative feedback in providing robustness.
source: This raises the intriguing possibility that Nodal positive feedback serves a similar purpose. Though dispensable for gradient formation per se, positive feedback may help to ensure that a gradient of the appropriate shape and intensity forms even in the face of mutations, environmental insults or signaling noise.
evidence: Speculative proposal based on parallel with Lefty findings
